Situations

You rarely need “roofing content.” You need to know what to do right now, in the situation you’re in. Start from the moment you’re facing.

If you are in an emergency right now Protect people first. Do not touch wet electrical equipment, do not walk through standing water to reach a breaker, do not stand beneath or puncture a sagging ceiling, and do not go onto a wet or storm-damaged roof. If there is danger, call your local emergency number.

Roofing decisions almost never begin with research. They begin with an event — a stain spreading across a ceiling tile, a storm that just passed, a proposal that doesn’t read right. This pillar organizes CRI’s guidance the way those moments actually arrive: by how much time you have, and what the next few hours or days will decide.

Each guide below is written to be usable while the problem is still happening — what to do first, what to protect, what to document before anything changes, and the decisions that are safe to defer. Every one lists its sources and carries its publication status, so you know how mature the guidance is before you rely on it.

Happening right now

Water is coming in and decisions cannot wait. These guides lead with the safety steps, then the ones that protect the building and the evidence.

Technical review pending

My Roof Is Leaking — What To Do Right Now

A commercial roof is leaking into your building. What to do in the first hour, what to protect, what to document, and the expensive mistakes people make while the water is still coming in.

  • Protect people first. Water near electricity is what injures people during a roof leak — not the water itself.
  • Never stand beneath, puncture, or disturb a sagging or bulging ceiling. Clear the area and get qualified help to evaluate it from a safe position.

The days that follow

The event has passed but the clock has not stopped. What gets documented, reported, and signed in this window shapes everything downstream.

Commercial Roof Insurance Claims: The Owner's Playbook

How commercial roof claims get evaluated — the paper trail adjusters work against, wind damage versus wear-and-tear, and the sequence from notice to settlement.

  • Claims are decided on documentation: pre-loss condition, dated damage evidence, and mitigation records.
  • The central dispute in most roof claims is storm damage versus wear-and-tear — policies generally cover accidental damage, not gradual deterioration, and your maintenance file is the counter-evidence.

Hurricane Preparation for Commercial Roofs

A preparation sequence for named storms: what to secure, document, and stage before landfall — and why the pre-storm file shapes the post-storm claim.

  • Hurricane prep is mostly documentation and drainage: record the roof's pre-storm condition, and make sure water can leave the roof.
  • A dated pre-storm photo record is evidence you cannot recreate afterward — disputed claims often turn on prior condition.

4 sources cited · Updated Jul 21, 2026

Storm Damage: The First 72 Hours

What to do after wind or hail hits your commercial roof — how to stay safe, what to document before anything changes, who to call, and the contract traps that follow a storm.

  • Nobody goes on the roof until it is safe and someone trained is there. A storm-damaged roof can look intact and not hold weight.
  • Document before anything changes — including before tarping. What you cannot photograph now, you cannot prove later.

When a situation needs professional eyes

Most situations have a reading answer and a looking answer. A guide can tell you what ponding water means; it cannot tell you whether the water on your roof is ponding, or whether the stain in unit 4B started above it. Reading is enough when you are orienting yourself, comparing options, or deciding what to ask. It stops being enough at a few specific points:

  • After any storm that touched the building — wind and hail damage is often invisible from the ground, and undocumented damage is difficult to claim later.
  • When water has reached the interior more than once — repeat leaks in the same area usually indicate a system problem, not a spot failure.
  • Before a capital decision — reserve studies, budget cycles, and repair-versus-replace calls all rest on the roof’s actual condition, not its age.
  • When a proposal recommends full replacement and you have no independent read — a documented condition report is how you check a recommendation against evidence.
  • Before buying or refinancing — the roof is frequently the least-inspected major system in a building at the moment it matters most.

A condition assessment is documentation, not a commitment: a walked roof, photos, and a written report that is yours to keep whether or not any work follows. CRI arranges these at no cost.

Request a roof condition assessment A documented roof walk, photographs, and a written condition report — no obligation, and no pressure standard: partners who pitch during an assessment lose the referral relationship.
